title: A command-line tool or bot that calls a public API
summary: A small Python CLI or chat bot that fetches data from a public API, handles errors and rate limits, caches responses and keeps its API key out of the code.
why: Almost every intern task touches an API. This proves you can read API documentation, make HTTP requests, handle failures and secrets responsibly, and test code that depends on the network.
brief:
Pick a free public API you find genuinely useful: weather, public transit arrivals, GitHub repositories, a library catalog, sports scores or rocket launches. Build a command-line tool (or a Discord or Slack bot, if you prefer) that answers one real question well, for example `nextbus 42 --stop Main` or `ghstats octocat --top 5`.

Constraints: if the API needs a key, read it from an environment variable and ship a `.env.example` file, never the key itself. Set a timeout on every request. Handle each failure case on purpose: no network, a 404 for a bad query, a 429 rate limit (back off and retry, honoring a Retry-After header when present) and a 5xx server error. Cache responses on disk for a few minutes so repeated commands are instant and you stay under the rate limit.

Tests must not call the real API. Mock the HTTP layer (with unittest.mock, or a library such as responses or respx) so the tests are fast and deterministic. This builds on the task manager project: reuse its shape of a core module plus a thin command-line layer.

milestones.title: Explore the API
tasks: Read the API documentation and make three requests with curl or the Recurse HTTP explorer
Save one real response as a JSON fixture file
Write down the endpoints, parameters, authentication method and rate limits you will use
milestones.doneWhen: A notes file lists your endpoints and their rate limit, next to a saved sample response.

milestones.title: Client module
tasks: Write a small client module with one function per endpoint
Read the key from an environment variable and stop with a helpful message if it is missing
Set a timeout on every request and turn HTTP errors into your own exception types
milestones.doneWhen: Calling a client function from a Python shell returns parsed data, and a wrong key produces a clear error message.

milestones.title: The command or bot
tasks: Build the CLI with argparse (or the bot's command handler)
Format output for people: a short table or a few lines, not raw JSON
Add a --json flag for machine-readable output
milestones.doneWhen: The tool answers its main question with one command in under two seconds on a normal connection.

milestones.title: Resilience and caching
tasks: Retry 429 and 5xx responses with exponential backoff, a cap on attempts and Retry-After support
Cache responses on disk with a time-to-live
Show a friendly message when offline
milestones.doneWhen: Running the same command twice within the cache window makes only one network request, confirmed by a log line.

milestones.title: Tests with mocks
tasks: Test parsing against the saved fixture
Mock the HTTP layer to simulate 200, 404, 429 followed by 200, 500 and a timeout
Test that the cache is used and that it expires
milestones.doneWhen: `pytest` passes with the network turned off.

stretch: Deploy the bot so it runs all the time on a free hosting tier
Add a scheduled daily summary message
Combine data from two APIs into one answer
rubric: A reviewer should find no API key or token anywhere in the repository or its history
A reviewer should see a timeout on every HTTP request
A reviewer should see 404, 429 and 5xx responses handled explicitly with clear messages
A reviewer should see tests that pass with the network disabled
A reviewer should see a cache that measurably reduces repeated requests
A reviewer should see a README that explains how to get a key and configure it
showcase: README: the question the tool answers, a GIF or sample output, setup (how to get an API key and set the environment variable), usage, and a 'How it handles failure' section
Link the API's documentation and note its rate limits
For a bot, include a screenshot of it working in a real server
resumeBullet: Built a Python CLI that answers real-time transit questions from a public REST API, with retry and backoff for rate limits, a disk cache that cut repeat requests by 90%, and fully mocked pytest tests.
interviewTalkingPoints: How you handled rate limits: backoff, a retry cap and the Retry-After header
Why tests should not call the real API, and how you mocked it
Where the cache lives, how long entries last, and the trade-off between freshness and speed
How you kept the API key out of the repository
